skill.name: Emotive words: spot them and say it neutrally
skill.why: Emotive words push your feelings. Spotting them lets you think for yourself.
skill.how: Find words loaded with feeling. Swap each for a calm word that means the same.

beats.say: Some words are picked to make you feel something.
We call them emotive words. They push your feelings.
Happy ones count too. They push you the other way.
To say it neutrally, keep what happened. Drop the feeling.
Don't change the facts. Closed is calm. Fixed is wrong!

encounters.frame: Ada Pennick's letter is going to the council, but the clerk says it needs to be calmer. The Puffentie agrees.
encounters.text: Dear Councillors, I am writing on behalf of the Bluster Bay Turtle Volunteers to ask you to cancel the licence that allows jet ski hire in the bay. For decades, the northern end of the bay has been a nesting beach for green turtles. Every summer, our volunteers count the nests, fence them off and watch the hatchlings scramble down to the water by moonlight. Since the hire shop opened in October, rangers have found fourteen injured turtles in the bay, most of them with cuts that match the shape of a propeller. My first draft of this letter included the following sentence: 'Reckless thrill-seekers on roaring jet skis have mown down fourteen defenceless turtles in our once-peaceful bay.' The council clerk has kindly pointed out that councillors are more likely to listen to the facts if they are not wrapped in so much feeling, and that the rangers' figures are powerful enough on their own. I have therefore agreed to rewrite it. I would be grateful if you could read the rangers' report before the vote on 12 December. Yours faithfully, Ada Pennick, turtle volunteer

encounters.frame: Two letters about the music festival are in today's Bugle. The Puffentie is sorting their phrases, and puffing furiously.
encounters.text: The council's plan to bring back the Bluster Rock Music Festival has divided the town, and this week the Bugle received two very different letters about it. The first came from Jojo Reyes, the lead singer of Red Dust Static, who wants the festival to return next autumn. She called it 'a joyous celebration of everything that makes our town special' and reminded readers that the 2019 festival attracted 6,000 visitors. Her letter also said the festival would bring money to local shops, and she asked readers to support it at the council meeting. The second came from Pat Grumbleton of Dune Street, who described the old festival as 'a deafening, sleepless nightmare' and complained about 'rowdy mobs' trampling his front garden. Pat said he had lived on Dune Street for forty years, and he asked the council to think of residents who need their sleep. The Bugle has decided to print both letters in full on page five. Both letters included some neutral details: the festival was held every autumn until 2019, it used a stage built on a flatbed truck, and it ran for two days. The council will vote on the plan at its meeting on 3 March, and residents are welcome to attend.

encounters.frame: Gus is writing up his mould experiment for the science fair judges. Wren says one word is too dramatic.
encounters.text: For his science fair project, Gus left five foods in sealed jars for fourteen days. The jars sat on the windowsill of the Soggy Biscuit's galley. The foods were white bread, an orange, cheese, a boiled potato and one of Mo's fish-finger custards. He photographed each jar at the same time every morning and measured how much of the surface was covered in mould. The bread grew mould first, on day three, and the orange was completely covered by day ten. Wren checked the jars each morning to make sure the lids were still tight. The cheese grew the least mould of the real foods, and Mo's custard grew none at all, which worried everyone. On day fourteen, Gus opened the jars to take samples, and a smell spread through the galley that was so strong Tully moved her hammock onto the deck. Mo said it reminded him of his cousin's football boots. The science fair judges have asked for reports that are calm and exact, because, as the head judge puts it, 'good science describes, it doesn't dramatise'. Gus has written most of his report in that style, but one word in his description of day fourteen still gives away how he felt.
encounters.prompt: Tap the emotive word in Gus's report. Then choose a neutral word.
encounters.success: 'Strong' keeps how powerful the smell was. It just drops the push to feel sick.

encounters.frame: Maxx is reading out a news story about Bluster Rock Primary on his stream. The Puffentie can barely keep still.
encounters.text: Maxx it out, Vantafam! Big news today from Bluster Rock Primary. The school has announced that its brass bell, which has rung at the start of every lunch for sixty years, will be replaced next term by a robot that sings. The robot is about the size of a toaster, and it will sit on the staffroom roof. Principal Okafor says it can sing twelve different songs, including one about the canteen. Some students have started a petition to keep the bell, and so far it has forty names on it. The bell itself will be polished and put in a glass case in the school foyer. Of course, my channel has its own take on the story. My writers came up with this headline: 'Heartless principal ruthlessly dumps beloved bell for screeching tin-can robot.' Is it a bit much? Maybe. But that's Maxx-imum content! Some of you, especially the haters, have asked whether I would ever swap my alarm clock for a singing robot. Never, Vantafam. Nobody sings like me. The Bugle has asked to use the story too, but its editor wants the headline rewritten so that it reports the news without telling readers how to feel. Smash that heart button like it owes you money! Stay gold!
encounters.prompt: Which says Maxx's headline neutrally?
encounters.success: It keeps who is replacing what with what. 'Heartless', 'ruthlessly', 'beloved' and 'screeching tin-can' are gone.

options.text: Cruel principal coldly ditches cherished bell for a clanking machine.
options.reason: 'Cruel', 'coldly', 'cherished' and 'clanking' still push you to feel upset. It's emotive.

options.text: Principal replaces the school bell with a singing robot.
Principal adds a singing robot beside the school bell.
options.reason: This changes the facts. The robot is replacing the bell, not joining it.

options.text: Clever principal boldly upgrades the bell to a dazzling singing robot.
options.reason: 'Clever', 'boldly' and 'dazzling' push an admiring feeling. That's emotive too.

encounters.frame: Maxx is boasting about his painting again. The Bugle wants one plain sentence for its news page.
encounters.text: Maxx it out, Vantafam! I have the most incredible news. Last night, at the Bluster Rock Art Auction, my painting 'Gold on Gold' was sold to a mystery collector from overseas. The painting is two metres wide and covered in real gold leaf. The buyer has not been named, but they have 'excellent taste, obviously'. The auction raised $95,000 in total, from forty-two paintings. Let me say that again, louder, for the haters at the back: my genius, jaw-dropping painting sold for a mind-blowing $40,000! That is more than any painting has ever sold for at the Bluster Rock auction, and it's the second year in a row that I've broken the record. I painted it in under ten minutes, using a brush made from my own hair, which I think we can all agree is the most important hair in the world. As always, every cent goes to the Maxx Vantablack Rescue Fund. The Bugle wants to report the sale on its news page tomorrow, but its editor has asked for one plain sentence that tells readers the facts without any of my sparkle. Boring! Two Xs, because one X is for losers! Stay gold!
encounters.prompt: Build a neutral version of Maxx's sentence about the sale. Keep it in his words, so start with 'My'.
encounters.success: 'My painting sold for $40,000' keeps every fact. 'Genius', 'jaw-dropping' and 'mind-blowing' only add sparkle.

body.reason: Keep the facts, the painting, the sale and the price, and leave out every word that adds sparkle.
